parole.significato: only used in 'sto qua and 'sto qui
parole.testo: Clipping of esto, from Latin istum, accusative masculine singular of iste (“that”, pronoun), of Proto-Indo-European origin. Compare questo, codesto and stesso.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form a feminine singular noun, usually a deverbal
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -am, from Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂ (forms action nouns).

parole.significato: used, with a stem, to form the third-person singular present tense of -are verbs
parole.testo: From Latin -at.

parole.significato: used, with a stem, to form the second-person singular imperative of -are verbs
parole.testo: From Latin -ā.

parole.significato: used, with a stem, to form the first-person singular, second-person singular and third-person singular present subjunct…
parole.testo: From Latin -(e/i)am, -(e/i)ās, -(e/i)at.

parole.significato: used, with a stem, to form the third-person singular imperative of -ere verbs, and of those -ire verbs that do not inse…
parole.testo: From Latin -(e/i)at.

parole.significato: -able (that can be …ed; that is worthy to be …ed)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -ābilis. See also -évole.

parole.significato: used to derive nouns with an instrumental connotation
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -āculum. Partly from the Latin instrument noun suffix -culum in cases where it was attached to first-conjugation verb stems ending in -ā-. Partly from the Latin diminutive suffix -ulus in cases where it was attached to noun stems ending in -āc- (e.g. loquāculus ← loquāx).
From Latin -āceum, -āceam, the accusative singular of -āceus, -ācea.
From Latin -aceum/-aceam, the accusative singular of -aceus/-acea. Doublet of -azzo.

parole.significato: used to form adjectives expressing a tendency or inclination to the action of the root; -ish, -y, -acious
parole.testo: From Latin -ācem.

parole.significato: added to nouns to form adjectives to denote "made out of" or "resembling"; -aceous
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -acĕus. Compare Italian -accio.

parole.significato: added to adjectives to form nouns denoting a quality, typically negative; -cy, -ness
parole.testo: From Latin -aginem.

parole.significato: -age; forms nouns indicating an action or result related to the root verb
parole.testo: From Latin -āticum, probably through Old Occitan -atge; cf. also Old French -age, Sicilian -aju. Doublet of -atico.

parole.significato: used to create female collective nouns, often pejorative
parole.testo: From Latin -ālia, the neuter plural of -ālis.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the first-person singular past historic of -are verbs
parole.testo: From Latin -āvī, via -āī. Example: Italian lodai, from Latin laudāvī.

parole.significato: forms feminine agent nouns from verbs
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -āria, feminine of -ārius. Compare the doublet -aria. Example: Italian operaia, from Latin operāria.

parole.significato: added to nouns to form agent nouns
parole.testo: From Latin -ārius. Compare the borrowed doublet -ario, as well as -iere, borrowed from (Old) French. Example: Italian operaio, from Latin operārius.

parole.significato: used to form the names of those who practice a profession or perform an activity
parole.testo: From Latin -āriolus, diminutive of -ārius.

parole.significato: added to nouns to form adjectives, often specifically relational adjectives; -al
parole.testo: From Latin -ālis.
Learned borrowing from New Latin -algia.

parole.significato: used to form collective nouns from simple nouns, often with pejorative connotation
parole.testo: From Latin -āmen, an extended form of -men.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the first-person plural past historic of regular -are verbs
parole.testo: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *-āvmus, from Latin -āvimus.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the gerund of regular -are verbs
parole.testo: From Latin -andus. Compare Spanish and Portuguese -ando and Romanian -ând.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the third-person plural present tense of regular -are verbs
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ant.

parole.significato: forms adjectives from locations, meaning “of, from or related to the location”
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ānus (adjectival derivational suffix).

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the present participle of regular -are verbs
parole.testo: From Latin -antem.

parole.significato: added to nouns and adjectives to indicate a state or condition; -ance; -ancy
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -antia. Compare Spanish -anza, Portuguese and Catalan -ança, French -ance.
From Late Latin -archa, from Latin -archēs, from Ancient Greek -άρχης (-árkhēs), from ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “rule”, “government”).
From Latin -archia, from Ancient Greek -αρχία (-arkhía).

parole.significato: the infinitive ending of most regular verbs; also, a productive suffix forming new verbs from nouns
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -āre.

parole.significato: suffix forming adjectives, often specifically relational adjectives, from nouns
parole.testo: From Latin -āris.

parole.significato: -ary; added to nouns to create relational adjective forms and show relation
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -ārius. Compare the inherited doublet -aio.
Borrowed from Latin -ārium.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the third person plural past historic of regular -are verbs
parole.testo: From Latin -ārunt, short counterpart to -āvērunt. In the thirteenth century, the Italian form was -aro, which later was extended to -arono under the influence of verb endings like -ano and -ono. Example: Italian lodarono, from Latin laudā(vē)runt.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the second-person past historic and imperfect subjunctive of regular -are verbs
parole.testo: From Latin -āstis, short counterpart to -āvistis. For example, Italian lodaste, < Latin laudā(vi)stis.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the second-person singular past historic of regular -are verbs
parole.testo: From Latin -āstī, short counterpart to -āvistī. For example, Italian lodasti, < Latin laudā(vi)stī.
From Latin -astrum, accusative singular of -aster. Cognate to French -âtre and Spanish -astro.

parole.significato: used to form verbal nouns, derived from regular -are verbs, expressing an instance of the action expressed by the verb;…
parole.testo: Nominalization of the past participle form of Etymology 1.

parole.significato: used with a suffix to form the feminine plural past participle of regular -are verbs
parole.testo: Feminine plural of -ato. Inherited from Latin -ātās, feminine accusative plural of -ātus.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the second-person plural present and imperative of regular -are verbs
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ātis (second-person plural present active indicative ending). The imperative comes from Latin -ate.

parole.significato: used to derive adjectives with a meaning of “of, pertaining to”
parole.testo: Most likely inherited from Latin -āticus. Doublet of -aggio, from Old Occitan or Old French. parole.significato: used with a stem to form the past participle of regular -are verbs
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ātus (second declension), from Proto-Italic *-ātos. Inherited from Latin -ātus (fourth declension), from Proto-Italic *-tus.

parole.significato: forms the noun denoting the result, product, object, or effect of the action expressed by a verb
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ātum (second declension), from the substantivized neuter singular of perfect passive participles in -ātus.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the third-person imperfect of regular -are verbs
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ābat.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the first-person plural imperfect of regular -are verbs
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ābāmus.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the third-person plural imperfect of regular -are verbs
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ābant.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the second-person plural imperfect of regular -are verbs
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ābātis.
Variant of the suffix -accio, from Latin -āceus.

parole.significato: -cide (denoting a person or substance that kills)
parole.testo: From Latin -cīda, from the base of caedō (“to cut, strike, kill”).
From Latin -cīdium, from the base of caedō (“to cut, strike, kill”).
Borrowed from Latin cyta, from Ancient Greek κύτος (kútos).
From Latin -dactylus, derived from Ancient Greek δάκτυλος (dáktulos, “finger”).
Cf. dotto, from Latin ductus.

parole.significato: the infinitive ending of a family of irregular verbs conjugated similarly to -ere ones
parole.testo: From Latin dūcere. See also ducere.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the third-person present of regular -ere verbs and those -ire verbs that don't take "isco"
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -it and -et.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form a masculine or feminine singular noun.
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -em.
Inherited from Latin -icius. Doublet of -izio, which was borrowed. Far rarer than -iccio, from Latin -īcius.

parole.significato: used to form verbs from adjectives or nouns
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin -izāre. Doublet of -izzare, which was borrowed. Cognate with Sicilian -ijari.

parole.significato: used with an infinitive stem to form the conditional mood.
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin hĕbui / (h)ĕ(bu)i, which stems from classical Latin habuī, first-person singular perfect of habeō. See -erei.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the first-person singular past historic of regular -ere verbs
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ēvī.

parole.significato: suffix used to form noun diminutives from nouns (including proper nouns) and sometimes adjectives and verbs, often with…
parole.testo: From Latin -ellus.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the first-person plural past historic of regular -ere verbs
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin *hebuimus, which stems from classical Latin habuimus, first-person plural perfect of habeō. See -eremmo.

parole.significato: Forms adjectives denoting age from numerals
parole.testo: Back-formation from centenario, from Latin centēnārius, from centēnus + -ārius. Cognate with French -enaire, Portuguese -enário, Spanish -enario.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the gerund of regular -ere and -ire verbs
parole.testo: From Latin -endus, -iendus. Compare Spanish and Portuguese -iendo and Romanian -ind.
From Latin -ennis (like in biennis, triennis), derived from annus (“year”).

parole.significato: forms nouns from numbers, meaning "period of ~ years"
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -ennium, from -ennis (annus + -is) + -ium.

parole.significato: used to create adjectives and nouns that denote ethnonyms, like parmense, from Parma or statunitense, from Stati Uniti
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Latin -ēnsis (“originating in”), whence also the inherited Italian doublet -ese.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the present participle of regular -ere and -ire verbs
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -entem.

parole.significato: added to verbs to form abstract nouns; -ency; -ence; -ance
parole.testo: From Latin -ĕntia. Compare French -ence, Portuguese -ença, -ência, Romanian -ință, -ență, Spanish -enza, -encia.

parole.significato: used to form adjectives referring to the qualities of the root noun; -en, -eous, -ean
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -eus.

parole.significato: used to form adjectives and nouns expressing relation to the root noun; -an, -ean
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -aeus, from Ancient Greek -αῖος (-aîos).

parole.significato: stem, to form the infinitive of some Italian verbs

parole.significato: stem, to form the infinitive of some Italian verbs

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the third-person singular conditional of regular -are and -ere verbs

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the third-person plural conditional of regular -are and -ere verbs
parole.testo: From -er- + -ebbero. * -er- is the reduced form of the Italian infinitive endings -are and -ere. * -ebbero stems from Vulgar Latin hĕbuerunt, which stems from classical Latin habuērunt, third-person plural perfect of habeō. See Italian -erei.
Inherited from Late Latin -āricius, from -ārius + -icius, whence respectively Italian -aio and -eccio.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the first-person singular conditional of regular -are and -ere verbs

The Italian conditional mood stems from a Vulgar Latin periphrastic verb form consisting o

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the first-person plural conditional of regular -are and -ere verbs
parole.testo: From -er- + -emmo. * -er- is the reduced form of the Italian infinitive endings -are and -ere. * -emmo stems from Vulgar Latin hĕbuimus, which stems from classical Latin habuimus, first-person plural perfect of habeō. See -erei.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the first-person plural future of regular -are and -ere verbs
parole.testo: A combination of the verb suffix -are (where the a was reduced to e) or -ere with Latin habēmus.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the second-person plural conditional of regular -are and -ere verbs
parole.testo: From -er- + -este. * -er- is the reduced form of the Italian infinitive endings -are and -ere. * -este stems from Vulgar Latin hĕbuistis, which stems from classical Latin habuistis, second-person plural perfect of habeō. See Italian -erei.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the second-person singular conditional of regular -are and -ere verbs
parole.testo: From -er- + -esti. * -er- is the reduced form of the Italian infinitive endings -are and -ere. * -esti stems from Vulgar Latin hĕbuisti, which stems from classical Latin habuistī, second-person singular perfect of habeō. See Italian -erei.

parole.significato: added to nouns to form other nouns meaning "place of" (an art, craft, or practice)
used with a stem to form the first-person singular future of regular -are verbs
parole.testo: A combination of the verb suffix -are (where the a was reduced to e) or -ere with ho, first person singular present indicative of avere. parole.significato: forms adjectives (sometimes used as nouns) that indicate relationship, membership, quality
parole.testo: From Late Latin, Vulgar Latin -iscus. Cognates: see Proto-Germanic *-iskaz.
Inherited from Latin -ēnsem (“originating in”), whence also Italian -ense. Cognate with Sicilian -isi.
From Latin -ēsimus, exhibited in the numerals from 20-90, as well as the hundreds and thousands.
From Latin -issa, from Ancient Greek -ισσα (-issa).

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the second-person plural past historic and imperfect subjunctive of regular -ere verbs
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin hĕbuistis, which stems from classical Latin habuistis, second-person plural perfect of habeō. See -ereste.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the second-person singular past historic of regular -ere verbs
parole.testo: From Vulgar Latin hĕbuisti, which stems from classical Latin habuistī, second-person singular perfect of habeō. See -eresti.
From Latin -ēta, plural of -ētum. Compare -eto.
From Latin -ētum. Cognate to French -aie.

parole.significato: suffix used to form melioratives, diminutives, and hypocoristics
parole.testo: From Late Latin -ittus.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the third-person singular imperfect of regular -ere verbs
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ēbat.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the first-person plural imperfect of regular -ere verbs
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ēbāmus.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the third-person plural imperfect of regular -ere verbs
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ēbant.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the second-person plural imperfect of regular -ere verbs
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ēbātis.

parole.significato: added to adjectives to form abstract nouns; -ity; -ness
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -itia, whence also Italian -izia, a borrowed doublet. Cognate with Sicilian -izza.
From Latin -phagus, from Ancient Greek φάγος (phágos, “glutton”), from φαγεῖν (phageîn, “to eat”).
From Latin -ficāre, apophonic compound form of faciō (“to do, make”).
From Latin -fōrmis, from fōrma (“form”).

parole.significato: used to form a noun that removes, exterminates, or expels; -fuge
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -fugus.
Borrowed from Latin genitus.
Borrowed from Latin -ger, from gerō (“to carry, to bear”).

parole.significato: used to form the plural of nouns ending in -o
parole.testo: There are two competing theories: # From Latin -ī, nominative plural of masculine nouns in -us. # From Latin -ōs, accusative plural of the same nouns, according to the sound change -os > -oi > -i (compare the pronoun vi).

parole.significato: forms surnames from proper names, occupations, etc.
parole.testo: Perhaps from the Latin genitive singular ending -ī of masculine nouns in -us.

parole.significato: derives abstract nouns denoting a state or condition from adjectives or nouns
parole.testo: From Ancient Greek -ία (-ía).
From Latin -ia, ultimately from the same source as above.
From Latin -ālis, used with nouns ending in -i-.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the first-person plural present, present subjunctive and imperative of regular -are, -ere and…
parole.testo: From Latin -eāmus (first-person plural present subjunctive suffix of the e-conjugation) and -iāmus (same of the i-conjugation). parole.significato: enlarged form of -ano, usually indicating a relationship of position, possession, or origin; often added to proper nouns
parole.testo: From Latin -iānus.

parole.significato: -ible (that can be …ed; that is worthy to be …ed)
parole.testo: Possibly borrowed from Latin -ibilis. Compare the inherited doublet -évole.

parole.significato: -ify; used to derive verbs related to a root noun or adjective
parole.testo: From the Latin verb ending -icāre. By surface analysis, -ic(o) (“-ic”, adjective-forming derivational suffix) + -are (verbal suffix).

parole.significato: used to derive verbs with a frequentative connotation
parole.testo: From Latin -iculāre.

parole.significato: A slightly diminutive-pejorative suffix used to form adjectives and nouns, denoting approximation.

parole.significato: a slightly diminutive-pejorative suffix used to form adjectives and nouns, denoting approximation

From Latin -idēs m (patronymic suffix; plural: -idae), from Ancient Greek -ίδης m (-ídēs, patronymic suffix; plural: -ίδαι (-ídai)).
From Latin -is f (genitive: -idis), from Ancient Greek -ῐς f (-ĭs) (genitive: -ῐδος (-ĭdos); plural: -ῐδες (-ĭdes)).
From Latin -idus.

parole.significato: forms nouns and adjectives indicating geographical origin

parole.significato: used to form collective and pejorative nouns
parole.testo: From Latin -īlĭa, plural neuter of -īlis.
Confluence of Latin -īneus and -ignus. Compare Sicilian -ignu.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the first-person singular past historic of regular -ire verbs
parole.testo: From Latin -īvī (via -īī). Example: Italian finii, from Latin finivi.

parole.significato: used to form nouns indicating locations that host animals or objects
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -īle (forming names of enclosures for animals; more generally, forming names of places where certain goods are stored).
From Latin -īlem.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the first-person plural past historic of regular -ire verbs
parole.testo: From Latin -īvimus (via -īvmus). Example: Italian finimmo, from Latin finivimus.

parole.significato: inflectional suffix used to form diminutives of feminine nouns
parole.testo: From Latin -īna.

parole.significato: used to derive adjectives and nouns indicating a state or condition
parole.testo: Via Vulgar Latin *-ingus, from Proto-West Germanic *-ing, from Proto-Germanic *-ingaz (“belonging to; coming from”).
From Latin -īnus. Compare English -ine.

parole.significato: used with verb roots to derive nouns with durative, intensive or frequentative connotation; -le
parole.testo: Unknown. Perhaps from Latin -ērium.

parole.significato: added to nouns and adjectives to form adjectives meaning “having the quality of”; -y
parole.testo: From Latin -ius.

parole.significato: forms the name of chemical elements; -ium
parole.testo: Borrowed from New Latin -ium.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the third-person singular past historic of regular -ire verbs
parole.testo: From Latin -īvit via Vulgar Latin -īut.

parole.significato: used, with a stem, to form the infinitive of some Italian verbs
parole.testo: From Latin -ire.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the third-person plural past historic of regular -ire verbs
parole.testo: From Latin -īverunt (via -īru). In the thirteenth century, the Italian form was -iro, which later was extended to -irono under influence of verb endings like -ano and -ono. Example: Italian finirono, from Latin finiverunt.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the first-person singular future of regular -ire verbs
parole.testo: A combination of the verb suffix -ire with ho, first person singular present indicative of avere. This traces back to a Vulgar Latin periphrastic construction of forming the future using the infinitive of the verb + habeō, e.g. seguirò, from Vulgar Latin *sequīre habeō.

parole.significato: used with some -ire verbs to make the present stem
parole.testo: Inherited from Latin -ēscere.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the third-person singular present of most regular -ire verbs
parole.testo: A form of the infix -isc-, from Latin -ēscō, in this case -ēscit. Cognates include Romanian -eşte, Sicilian -isci, Spanish -ece.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the second-person singular present of most regular -ire verbs
parole.testo: A form of the infix -isc-, from Latin -ēscō, in this case -ēscis. Cognates include Romanian -eşti, Sicilian -isci, Spanish -eces.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the first-person singular present of most regular -ire verbs
parole.testo: A form of the infix -isc-, from Latin -ēscō. Cognates include Romanian -esc, Sicilian -isciu, Spanish -ezco.
Inherited from Latin -ismus.

parole.significato: added to adjectives to form absolute superlatives
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -issimus. Compare Spanish -ísimo and Portuguese -íssimo which are partly based on the Italian forms.
Borrowed from Latin -ista, from Ancient Greek -ιστής (-istḗs).

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the second-person plural past historic and imperfect subjunctive of regular -ire verbs
parole.testo: From Latin -īvistis (via -īsti). Example: Italian finiste, from Latin finivistis.

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the second-person past historic of regular -ire verbs
parole.testo: From Latin -īvisti (via -īsti). Example: Italian finisti, from Latin finivisti.

parole.significato: used to create adjectives and nouns that indicate "belonging to"; -ite
parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin -īta, from Ancient Greek -ίτης (-ítēs).

parole.significato: used to form abstract nouns that correspond to English words ending in -ity or -ness
parole.testo: From earlier -itate, from Latin -itātem with voicing of the second /-t-/. Reduced to -ità in modern Italian via apocope. Compare Old Italian -itude > modern -Italian -itù. Compare soccida for a different output.

parole.significato: used to form verbs, sometimes iterative, from adjectives or other verbs

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the past participle of regular -ire verbs

parole.significato: used to form abstract nouns that correspond to English words ending in -ity or -ness

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the third-person singular imperfect of regular -ire verbs

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the first-person plural imperfect of regular -ire verbs

parole.significato: used with a stem to form the third-person plural imperfect of regular -ire verbs

parole.significato: added to adjectives to form abstract nouns; -ness, -ity, -ice, -ship

Inherited from Late Latin thius, from Ancient Greek θεῖος (theîos). Compare Spanish tío, Portuguese tio, Sicilian ziu, Sardinian tiu or tziu, Venetan sio.
From Latin zirbus, itself from Arabic ثَرْب (ṯarb).
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin zizania, from Ancient Greek ζιζάνια (zizánia), plural of ζιζάνιον (zizánion).
From Latin socculus, diminutive of soccus (“sock, slipper”). Compare Sicilian zòcculu and Spanish zócalo.
Inherited from Latin sulphur, sulfur. For the initial z- compare also zoccolo. Cognate with Sicilian sùrfuru and Venetan solfaro.

Borrowed from New Latin zooecium, derived from Ancient Greek ζῷον (zōîon, “animal”) + οἶκος (oîkos, “house”).

parole.significato: to have a limp, to walk with a limp
parole.testo: From zoppo + -icare, or inherited from Vulgar Latin *cloppicāre, from Late Latin cloppus. Compare Sicilian zuppijari.

From Vulgar Latin, Late Latin cloppus, perhaps ultimately imitative of a limping person. The Italian was possibly altered by influence from zanca. Compare Romanian șchiop, cf. also Catalan and Occitan esclop, Old French clop and Sicilian zoppu.
From New Latin/translingual Zostera.
From Late Latin cucutia (via metathesis and apheresis), from Latin cucurbita (“gourd”). Doublet of cocuzza and cucurbita.

From Vulgar Latin *sūfilāre, from Latin sībilāre, whence also the doublets sibilare and sobillare. Cognate with Corsican zifulà, Venetan sifołar, Romansh tschüvler, tschivlar, Norman sûfflier, Walloon xhufler (Old French sufler).

parole.significato: one of several types of soup
parole.testo: From Late Latin suppa, borrowed from Proto-Germanic *supô, *suppa (“slice of soaked bread; soup”) (whence English soup).
Probably a dialectal variant of girlo crossed with Vulgar Latin *currūlus, diminutive of currus (“chariot; plough rollers”).
